questions.question: What kind of function $f\colon I\to\mathbb{R}$ is considered?
options: An unbounded function on any set
Only a finite sequence
Only a function with domain $\mathbb{N}$
A bounded function on a bounded interval $I$

questions.question: What would go wrong if two different numbers both satisfied the Riemann integrability condition for the same function?
options: The function would become constant.
The partition would have no subintervals.
The interval length would be zero.
The integral value would not be well-defined.

questions.question: Which type of function is Riemann integrable on closed bounded intervals?
options: All unbounded functions
Only constant sequences
Continuous functions
Only functions with values in $\mathbb{Z}$

questions.question: What boundedness condition is required for the Riemann integral?
options: $f$ must be bounded on $I$.
$f$ must be undefined on $I$.
$I$ must be an infinite sequence.
$s$ must depend on one chosen sample point only.

questions.question: What must happen to the Riemann sums for $f$ to be integrable with integral $s$?
options: Only one chosen sample point must give exactly $s$ for $n = 1$.
The sums must be undefined for large $n$.
Fine subdivisions give sums within $\varepsilon$ of $s$ for any sample choice.
The sums must depend only on the left endpoint of $I$.

questions.question: Which statement about sample points is supported?
options: The integral value changes whenever a sample point changes.
The integral value is independent of the choice of sample points $x_i^*$.
Sample points are not allowed in Riemann sums.
Only endpoints may be used as sample points.

questions.question: For a constant function $f(x) = 3$ on an interval of total length $2$, what value should every Riemann sum have?

Let $f$ be defined on a bounded closed interval $I$. For every $\varepsilon>0$, all tagged Riemann sums with sufficiently small mesh differ from $4$ by less than $\varepsilon$. What does this imply about the Riemann integral of $f$ on $I$?
options: $f$ has reciprocal $4^{-1}$.
The Riemann integral of $f$ on $I$ is $4$.
The interval $I$ has exactly $4$ points.
The sample points must all equal $4$.

questions.question: Which assumption is essential for Riemann integrability in this definition?
options: Boundedness of the function
That the function is a sequence
That the interval has no endpoints
That only one Riemann sum exists

questions.question: Why does the definition use “any” sample point $x_i^*\in J_i$?
options: To avoid using partitions.
So the limit doesn't depend on a special sample choice.
To require all sample points to be equal.
To make $s$ depend on the first subinterval only.

questions.question: Which statement correctly applies the definition to a proposed value $s$?
options: It is enough that one coarse subdivision has sum exactly $s$.
The value $s$ must be chosen separately for each sample point.
The condition only checks whether $f$ is unbounded.
For every $\varepsilon \gt 0$, fine subdivision sums are within $\varepsilon$ of $s$.

questions.question: A bounded monotone function is given on a closed interval. What can be concluded?
options: It must be discontinuous everywhere.
It has no Riemann sums.
Its integral is always $0$.
It is Riemann integrable.

questions.question: Which function is Riemann integrable on the given interval?
options: $f(x)=x$ for rational $x$, $f(x)=0$ for irrational $x$, on $[0,1]$

questions.question: Which subdivisions are used in the stated integrability condition?
options: Only one fixed subdivision with $n=1$
Unbounded intervals only
Partitions with overlapping subintervals
Regular subdivisions with sufficiently large $n$

questions.question: What must be true for every $\varepsilon \gt 0$ in the integrability definition?
options: One arbitrary sum must equal $0$
The function must become unbounded
The sample points must all be endpoints.
Fine Riemann sums are within $\varepsilon$ of $s$.

questions.question: Let $f(x)=1/x$ for $0<x\le1$ and $f(0)=0$. Why is $f$ not Riemann integrable on $[0,1]$, although it is continuous on $(0,1]$?
options: It is unbounded on $[0,1]$, and the Riemann integral is defined only for bounded functions.
It is discontinuous at $0$, and a function with a discontinuity is never Riemann integrable.
It is Riemann integrable after all, with integral equal to the improper integral $\int_0^1\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{x}$.
The value $f(0)=0$ was chosen badly: with $f(0)=1$ instead, $f$ would be Riemann integrable on $[0,1]$.

questions.question: Let $a<b$. Which function need not be integrable, either as a Riemann integral on $[a,b]$ or as a convergent improper integral on $(a,b)$?
options: The function $(x-a)^{-1/2}$ on $(a,b)$.
A function that is differentiable on $(a,b)$.
A monotone function on $[a,b]$.
A difference $g-h$ of two increasing functions on $[a,b]$.

questions.question: For $f(x)=5$ on an interval of length $4$, what is the Riemann integral value?
Why must the integral value be independent of sample-point choices?
options: The definition forbids sample points
Sample choices in fine subdivisions approach the same $s$.
Only left endpoints are allowed
The value $s$ is chosen after each sample point.

questions.question: Let $D$ be the Dirichlet function on $[0,1]$ ($D=1$ on rationals, $D=0$ on irrationals). For regular partitions, which statement is correct?
options: Upper and lower sums both tend to $1$, so $D$ is integrable.
Left sums tend to $1$ and right sums tend to $0$.
Left and right Riemann sums both tend to $1$, yet $D$ is not Riemann integrable.
Left and right Riemann sums agree in the limit, so $D$ is integrable with integral $1$.
